en: Preface to the Commentary on the *Benevolent Kings’ Protection of the Nation Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* I have heard that the True Limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) is tranquil and vast, transcending defilement and purity within the realm of form and mind;

the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) is empty and expansive, surpassing cultivation and realization upon the stages of principle and wisdom. Profound, void, and luminously reflective, its wondrous essence is concentrated and eternal, uniquely manifesting the myriad [phenomena].

It is like an elephant that is neither many nor one; it stands preeminent throughout the ten directions yet is not dualistic. This is truly because it is not an arising through conditions of either unity or multiplicity;
defilement and purity stand side by side in mutual integration. Since the essence of cultivation and realization is emptiness, cause and effect are both forgotten as they penetrate one another.
Thus, there is emptiness within emptiness, and emptiness that is not empty; there is existence within emptiness, and existence that is not existent. Not...
There is existence; there is non-constancy; it is not empty of emptiness; emptiness is not annihilation. Because it is not annihilation, it is true emptiness (*śūnyatā*);
because it is not [merely] "when-to-be," it is wondrous existence (*prabhāsvara-bhāva*). Thus, the Way of wondrous existence and true emptiness is simultaneously compatible and mutually identical.
A single thought-moment inter-pervades and contains one another, until both containing and being contained are forgotten, and compatibility and identity are both transcended.
It stands in profound identity with the ultimate limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) and wondrously equals the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

Truly, it is the true ultimate nature within the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), far transcending the three vehicles and loftily surpassing the eight classes of beings. This is the most profound discourse of this sutra, which exhausts the subtle and completes the transformative.
This is a sublime and transcendent proclamation beyond the reach of words and thought.

Thus, our World-Honored One suddenly arrived at Vulture Peak with his elephant-mounted retinue; dragons and devas stood in attendance at the lion throne, while the assembly of sages gathered like clouds around the site of enlightenment.

The king and his ministers hasten like the wind toward the depths of principle; entering meditative concentration, their profound wisdom is like a sea of clear waves. Emitting light, it is as bright as the sun of wisdom in the sky of the nature.
Great Bodhisattvas from other realms offer exquisite flowers, incense, and lamps as offerings; the sovereigns of this land present precious banners, pennants, and canopies with sincere devotion.
They transform lands as numerous as motes of dust into pure realms and manifest jeweled terraces across billions of worlds. The Buddha sits upon the golden...
The lotus flows throughout lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, where all together discourse upon Prajñāpāramitā and are gathered back into this single spiritual source.

This King requested protection for the state; our Buddha replied with words of protecting the mind. He revealed the departure from marks to clarify the True, and through contemplating the emptiness of essence, he practiced transformation.
Realizing that one’s own body and the Buddha are identical in the single true mark, he established that principle and phenomenon are unified within the singular spirit.
The Profound (Xuan) is the pivot for protecting the nation and the essential path for stabilizing the realm.

Having realized that the fruit of protection lies in contemplating emptiness, and that Sudatta cultivated the causes to practice transformation, he thus elucidated both nature and non-nature as fundamentally being one spiritual awareness.
Through the fifty-two stages of true cultivation and the profound趣 (qù) of the fourteen gates, he provisionally manifested through assigned positions to subdue, sever, and realize.
Cultivation proceeds until the three provisional designations are all empty and the single characteristic is found to be without reality. At every turn, the wondrous light of prajñā rises;
at every step, one treads upon the ground of the principle of the true mark (*dharmatā*). Once the two protections are clear, the one truth shall manifest.

Therefore, the inquiry into the existence or non-existence of the two truths is intended to clarify that they are fundamentally neither one nor two. This was the verse of praise by the King, which the Tathāgata confirmed and perfected. For...
The principle-body is that upon which the practice of the Dharma relies; the function of wisdom is its capacity to illuminate the merit of the fruition.

These two—the protection of phenomena and the protection of principles—act in opposition; yet the essence and function of *prajñā* are non-dual. For this reason, this King repeatedly consulted the Protector of the Nation (*Rakṣa-rāṣṭra*).

The Tathāgata further manifested true compassion, saying: "The calamities and blessings of a land are summoned by the collective karma of sentient beings, while the fortunes and misfortunes of individuals arise from their distinct personal karma."
Manifestations: When the mind is upright, heaven is clear and earth is peaceful; when the mind is perverse, calamities and misfortunes arise.

If one wishes to cause a thousand disasters to cease instantly and ten thousand evils to vanish in secret, one must employ a hundred Dharma masters to uphold the Prajñāpāramitā, adorn a single *dharma-cakra* site, and make offerings to the images of the various saints.
Thus, when Śakra practiced this, Jambhaka immediately retreated; when Puming preached it...

That those who have cast aside worldly glory are worthy of such a performance is indeed for a profound reason. Yet, as the various kings attained understanding, each offered flowers according to their true nature;

the flowers transformed into precious terraces, and Buddha after Buddha together discoursed upon Prajñā. Sometimes a single flower manifested many lands, and many lands were contained within a single flower;
large and small, defiled and pure, they mutually encompassed one another. Truly, this may be called the ultimate exhaustion of the vast and expansive.

The profound essence of this [teaching] exhausts the inconceivable ocean-like assemblies. Thus we know that the merit of a single thought of pure faith surpasses the transformation and realization of *śrāvakas* as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
and the power of raising one’s mind to uphold [this teaching] exceeds the great virtue of bestowing the seven treasures.
This is truly not false. Previously, we discussed protecting the fruit, yet the cultivation of the causes was not fully exhausted. Furthermore, regarding the five patiences (*kṣānti*) and the ten...

The Grounds. This provides a detailed exposition of the subduing and severing [of afflictions], the realization and cultivation [of the path], the number of beings delivered, and the duration of the kalpas.

It extends even to the point where the Vajras of the five directions are commanded to recite mantras and provide protection. The intent is that the causal practices may reach great completion and that the sincere contemplation for protecting the state may reach its ultimate fulfillment.

Therefore, by relying on this to protect the state, one should contemplate the peace and harmony of the world; by depending on this to protect the fruition, for a time— [Note: The source text appears to be a fragment of a Buddhist ritual or commentary concerning the "Five-Direction Vajra" (Wǔfāng Jīngāng) rites for national protection.]
This carving of the *Bodhicittotpāda-sūtra* (The Sublime Realization of Bodhicitta) is undertaken so that the imperial domain may be eternally secure and the Emperor’s longevity may be boundless.
Apart from this Prajñāpāramitā, who else could provide such means? Nevertheless, considering the request for protection of the state, I shall first explain [the following].

Regarding the protection of the fruit: by taking the right mindfulness that protects the fruit as the golden wall and moat for protecting the state, one causes the seven calamities within the realm to vanish in secret and the five constants to spread far and wide.
This very profound resolve to protect the state serves as the wondrous medicine for transforming ordinary beings.
Thus, the four wisdoms above will indeed become perfectly luminous, and the three bodies will be realized instantaneously.

This means that protecting the state and protecting the fruit do not transcend the practice and realization of the stage of patience (*kṣānti-bhūmi*); they function in mutual dependence. Even so, once the profound and subtle mysteries were elucidated at that time, [the purpose was fulfilled].
Supreme benefits should reach those of the final age.

Anticipating the extinction of the Dharma, the Tathāgata earnestly cautioned and repeatedly exhorted that kings and ministers possessed the power to protect and uphold it. At that time, the king received these instructions;

weeping, he shook the three thousandfold world-system and immediately vowed to practice the Way, not restricting the fourfold assembly. The scripture is titled *The Ambrosial Medicine of the Dharma*, which they faithfully accepted.
It wards off illness and prolongs life; the merit of upholding it is equal to empty space.

It can protect kings, its efficacy surpassing that of city walls and moats. It may truly be called the ultimate compassionate mind, a great sorrow that universally saves. How magnificent is this sutra!
It universally encompasses the three faculties and contains all five flavors. One must look up to the profound mysteries of the Qin translation and the Tiantai [commentaries].

This commentary elucidates the profound and subtle mysteries. I humbly reflect that although the divine scriptures were translated during the Tang dynasty, later scholars have yet to peer into their depths.

Furthermore, while they speak of emptiness and existence, the underlying meaning is perfectly integrated; though the names "emptiness" and "existence" may appear identical, their essential natures differ.
Because subsequent generations have not fully grasped these points, I have deemed it honorable to provide this interpretation for them. From here on...

In the summer of the Wu-wu year, during the reign of the Divine Ancestor [Emperor Taizong], while returning from paying homage at Mount Qingliang, I was struck with alarm by news of the rebel slaves’ incursions and the loss of Fushun.
My eyes filled with grief at this calamity, and my sorrow flowed through me even in sleep.

Vowing to propagate this sacred tradition as a way to repay the national grace, I disregarded my own lack of refinement and committed these records to writing. At that time, my disciple Jingxian Zhonggong, a native of Guanzhong, [assisted].
He was more attentive than Zizhi, yet his aspirations remained unfulfilled as he passed away prematurely.

Last year, in the year Jisi, when the barbarians pressed against the capital, Guishe took refuge in a mountain cave and was likewise besieged; there, he reaffirmed his former resolve, hoping to eliminate the calamities.
Relying upon the Buddha’s protection, the Dharma-grandson Haike, together with his disciples Jimo and others, cast aside concern for life and body;
at night, supporting their aged frames, they observed the precepts in secret and returned to their original temple. Later, there was a disciple named Zhan Yizhun, a native of Yingzhou.
Having strictly refined the principles of the teachings, I saw that the surrounding obstacles had been resolved. Recalling my deep resolve to propagate the Sūtra, he urged me repeatedly.

To fulfill his vow regarding the "calamity-wood," I have once again scrutinized the text; wishing to express the meaning clearly and comprehensively, I have ventured to title this work a *ke-sū* (a topical outline).
It is my hope that readers will find in it the vision of one holding a candle, free from the weariness of seeking only the branches, and may thus rely upon it to penetrate the Sūtra. The Sūtra...

When one penetrates [this], the meaning is attained. Once the meaning is attained, the essence of Prajñā-wisdom becomes vividly manifest between the heart and mind, and brilliantly radiant within the realm of sensory objects.
Thus, Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa is not separate from this very place, and the Benevolent Kings are none other than myself.
O Sage Emperor! With the five patiences, you stand as a jade pillar supporting the heavens within the court; with the ten stages, you span as a golden beam across the seas beyond the borders.
The four barbarian tribes disperse their miasmic vapors in the realm of non-being, and the eight quarters turn their hearts toward the Great Luminous Kingdom.
I offer this meager tribute of gratitude.
This is the sincere devotion of a subject for the welfare of the nation and its people, and my profound earnestness in adorning the holy teachings.

This preface has been composed not out of a desire to display it in lecture halls and incur the laughter of the wise, but solely for the convenience of an eighty-year-old man to prevent his own forgetfulness.
It was written on the day of the Buddha’s Enlightenment in the third year of the Ming Chongzhen era, the year of Gengwu.
Founder of Cihui Temple in the Capital; Successor of the Xianshou School, the twenty-fifth generation patriarch;
Former Imperially Appointed Lecturer on Sutras and Shastras at the Imperial Altar.
